What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? The core tenet of atheism is a rejection of the supernatural, and consequently, a strong belief in the power of science to explain the natural world. If there is no God, then obviously there can be no acts of God, and everything that happens must be explicable through natural processes. Now, it's not that atheists think science has explained *everything* – far from it. In fact, most atheists are keenly aware of the limitations of our current scientific knowledge. We certainly don't understand everything! But, atheists generally believe that *everything* is *in principle* explainable through science. It's just a matter of time and effort, and continued scientific progress.To illustrate... imagine a scientist from the 1600s, before the age of modern chemistry. They might be baffled by the phenomenon of fire—how does it burn, what makes a log burst into flames, why does it produce heat? They might see the need for some kind of 'element' to make it possible, the “phlogiston theory”. They might even consider the possibility of it being magic! But today, with the advent of modern chemistry, we know that fire is a chemical reaction involving combustion, oxidation, and the involvement of volatile gases. As a result, the mystery of fire has been demystified, and it has been explained in terms of understandable and measurable scientific concepts.In the same way, an atheist would argue that any phenomenon that currently seems inexplicable, from the origins of the universe to the nature of consciousness, is *potentially* explained through science. It may not be easy to formulate solutions, and it's almost certain that there are still many unknowns—but in the atheistic worldview there is nothing that is *inherently* beyond the scope of scientific inquiry. We may not know the answers now, and it may take centuries or even millennia to reach the complete answer, but a core belief of atheism is that science provides the best mechanism to find those answers. There might be some specific hard problems, but ultimately, the answer is knowable.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? Well, yes and no. It's a bit like the monkey-to-human question. You’ve undoubtedly heard the joke about how if humans evolved from monkeys, why are there still monkeys? The answer is that modern monkeys and humans share a common ancestor, but it was neither a monkey nor a human. It was something else entirely. And it’s probably unrecognizable by either a modern human or monkey. Let’s put it this way: If humans and primates are on a family tree, then the common ancestor branched off a long time ago. Think of a modern family tree with a lot of different branches. Now, imagine that you can trace those branches all the way back to a particular origin point: ABOVE: A simplified phylogenetic tree SOURCE: My own diagram (please don't ask for citations) The concept of a universal and ancient common ancestor doesn't sound all that far-fetched once you understand the basis of how evolution actually happens. The theory of evolution posits that all living organisms are linked, and that over time this relationship changes gradually. It's not some sort of instant transformation, like from a monkey to a human! It occurs over very long time scales. Now, back to your question: elephants and mosquitoes. Do they share a common ancestor? Undoubtedly, yes. Can we say what it was? Absolutely not, as it’s difficult to say with certainty what the nature of that common ancestor would have been. It was probably a single-cell organism. A very, very, very, very long time ago.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? More or less, yes. The historical narrative surrounding Columbus is indeed still presented, albeit with a growing awareness of its complexities. It's a balancing act, really, between what we can definitively say and the narratives we tell, especially in a classroom setting. The emphasis seems to have shifted, at least in some circles, toward acknowledging the pre-Columbian voyages and the devastating impact of European contact on indigenous populations. ABOVE: Illustration depicting the impact of Columbus' arrival on indigenous populations. SOURCE: Various history textbooks. However, as a purely practical matter, it's hard to make people forget what they were taught at a young age. And I doubt the average American is going to remember all those nuanced details, anyway. It's like anything else. Everyone's heard of George Washington and Abraham Lincoln, but few people know all the specific details about, say, the Whiskey Rebellion or the Lincoln-Douglas debates. Then again, there might be a bit of survivorship bias at play here. The only people who are going to be able to actually argue about the historical facts are going to be people with a good education. And if you have a good education, you've probably already heard what they're going to say. Other people, who might have never even finished high school, aren't going to know about it. And even if they did, they're not going to be able to do anything about it.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? It depends. In my experience, most people don't give a damn. I've been to plenty of dinner parties where the food was great, the company was pleasant, and cheap paper plates and plastic utensils were the order of the day. And I'm fine with that. I've also been to fancy parties where they rented fine china, put out actual silverware, and had a waitstaff to clear the table. And I'm fine with that, too. Personally, I don't really care much either way, and I have a hard time imagining anyone actually caring. That being said, I do seem to recall my mom having a full set of 'good china' that she brought out for special occasions. Then again, it seemed like she only used it a few times per year. My guess is that like most people, she would have rather spent less time on the washing dishes, and more time on enjoying the company of friends and family. On the other hand, if you *are* specifically concerned about what the etiquette is, then it probably does matter. It comes down to the circumstances. If you're inviting a bunch of upper crust society folks to your house, then it might be considered rude. And I suppose if you're in that crowd yourself, you're likely to have a better sense of what's expected. But for most people, they probably aren't even going to notice. And if they did, then they certainly wouldn't care. Especially if the food was good.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. Okay, let's break this down. The core argument rests on the premise that everything requires a creator. If we accept this premise, then the question becomes, what created the creator? Theists usually posit that their god is the uncaused cause, which is supposed to be an adequate response. But if you introduce a mysterious being that requires no cause, why can't you simply say the same thing about the universe itself? The answer, as far as I can see, is that this is just a preference. People prefer a god because it offers comfort, meaning, or whatever. But intellectually, it's not a very strong argument. The other problem is that saying the Earth "had to be created" assumes that it's even possible for something to pop into existence without a cause. We certainly don't have any evidence that this does, or does not, happen, but that doesn’t make it impossible or a logical contradiction. So, if the universe is fundamentally caused by a higher power, and it is capable of existing as a result of that power, then the same logic can be applied to something that happened to precede it. The only problem is that we’re usually not able to conceive of how these things might happen. The best we can do is shrug our shoulders and chalk it up to the unknown.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) Okay, so let's break this down. The very nature of the question implies a degree of skepticism, a willingness to entertain possibilities, an inherent humility in acknowledging the vastness of the unknown. As an engineer, I appreciate that. It’s a core tenet of the scientific method, really. We're always refining our models, testing against new data, acknowledging that what we know today might be superseded by what we know tomorrow. That applies to the big questions, too.So, would anything convince me of the existence of a god(s)? That depends on what we mean by 'god'. I'm not talking about a bearded man in the sky, some sort of cosmic Santa Claus. If it's something more akin to a First Cause, a fundamental principle that underpins the universe, then perhaps. It would require concrete, verifiable evidence, something beyond faith or anecdotal claims. We’d need a testable hypothesis, the kind of thing you might see in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.The mere fact that I’m willing to consider the possibility makes me more agnostic than truly atheist, as you've observed. I wouldn't call myself an atheist in the absolute sense, because I don’t think anyone can just flat out say that a God does not exist. That's the trouble with such all or nothing stance on any kind of grand idea, it's inherently unscientific. Agnosticism to me suggests a cautious approach, an acknowledgement of the limitations of our current understanding. Like you said, being the wisest amongst us.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? Well, they're not. It's really as simple as that. You can find all sorts of people saying all sorts of nonsense online. But the vast majority of pilots, both commercial and military, are going to tell you that the Earth is a sphere. In fact, I'd be willing to bet that if you took a poll of all pilots, and even included a few of the ones you are referring to, you'd get less than 1% of them claiming it's flat. And that's the key to understanding the whole thing. It's a fringe conspiracy theory that has surprisingly stuck around and even has a few adherents in the present day. The fact that you know about it is simply because they're loud. Loud enough to get the attention of the algorithms that run social media. But that's not the same thing as being correct, of course. So while a tiny handful of pilots might subscribe to the idea, it's definitely not a widespread phenomenon. The vast majority of pilots are going to tell you the Earth is a sphere because they have the technical and scientific knowledge to understand these things, and they also have the practical experience of flying all over the world, and they've seen the curvature for themselves. Furthermore, they are the ones with a vested interest in knowing and understanding what the shape of the earth is. Without that knowledge, you simply can't fly.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? Let's address the elephant in the room, the central tenet on which Christianity rests: the resurrection. The claims you mention aren’t just a fringe theory; they directly contradict the core narrative. The New Testament is pretty clear about the whole resurrection thing. If Jesus just got resuscitated, then what happened to the tomb? Why would the apostles, allegedly having seen him resurrected, later die violent deaths for a lie? Doesn’t make much sense, does it? If I were a believer, I would find the idea that Jesus lived out his days peacefully in some other place rather insulting. Why wouldn't he show back up? Why leave his followers, the supposed founders of his religion, high and dry? What's the point of a secret eighty-year life? And if that's the case, why didn't anyone outside of the immediate disciples know? Wouldn't people have noticed a guy who seemed to be the same guy that had just been executed? Or at least heard rumors? The whole thing just seems convoluted and needlessly complex. There's no historical basis to support the idea either. But that's going to happen with these kinds of topics.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? Well, let’s unpack this a bit. The historical Jesus is a tricky subject, and there are, in fact, a great many books written about him. The Gospels, the core of the New Testament, are, of course, the primary sources. But even those are more or less anonymous. There is no “Gospel According to Matthew”, or “Mark”, or “Luke” as that is just a tradition based on very early attributions. They don't even claim to be written by people who knew Jesus personally. So, what was the inspiration? That’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? A few things come to mind. First, there’s the conviction of the early Christians. They believed, with a profound and impassioned certainty, that Jesus was the Messiah, the Son of God, and that He had risen from the dead. This was not a casual hobby; it was a belief that often brought with it persecution, ostracism, and even martyrdom. That kind of conviction generates words, and it leads people to go to great lengths to share what they “know”. Then there’s the nature of oral tradition. In the ancient world, before widespread literacy, stories were passed on through word of mouth. And as the message of Jesus spread, stories that might have drifted away from the facts became integral to the early Christian communities in those days.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? I'm not an expert on constitutional law, and I'm not a lawyer, but it seems to me that if a teacher is allowed to teach *about* evolution, she ought to be allowed to teach *against* it as well, provided that she doesn't bring up creationism as an alternative. And in fact, in the past, it was considered that the opposite was true. The 1925 Scopes Trial concerned a high school science teacher, John Scopes, who was charged with violating Tennessee's Butler Act, which had made it unlawful to teach the theory of evolution in any state-funded public schools. And yet in its defense, the ACLU brought in a team of prominent lawyers, and the trial became a media circus, pitting William Jennings Bryan, a three-time presidential candidate, and the prosecution, against Clarence Darrow, an agnostic and the defense. In the end, Scopes was found guilty and had to pay a paltry fine, but the case served as a catalyst in the evolution of public opinion, and by the 1960s, it was pretty much settled that teachers were allowed to teach evolution. But I digress. The real issue is that schools aren't meant to be places where kids are indoctrinated, but rather, places where they learn to think for themselves, to question things. And if evolution has a few holes in it, then students should be allowed to explore them. Any teacher should be allowed to show both sides of an issue.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? It's an interesting question, and one that keeps me up at night if I'm honest. I think the answer is complicated, but I'll take a stab at it. We're already seeing glimpses of the future. I mean, the military has been using holographic displays for ages, and self-driving cars are further along than many people realize. But those are just the precursors. True mass adoption of things like personal flying vehicles will be dependent on a confluence of factors. First, the technology has to get good enough and then cheap enough. We need the vehicles themselves to be safe, reliable, and affordable. Then there’s the infrastructure: How do we manage the traffic? Build the landing pads? And then, of course, there's regulation. The FAA is famously cautious. I don't blame them, really. Better safe than sorry. But they're not exactly known for speed. Think of it this way: Building codes and aviation regulations don’t update overnight. And even then, if safety and infrastructure are sorted, a lot of future technologies will still depend on the economics.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? I have to admit, that’s a genuinely interesting question, and one that I’ve given quite a bit of thought. Obviously, the answer depends on a whole host of factors that are constantly in flux, such as the current political climate, the specific issues that are dominating the news cycle at any given time, and, of course, both candidates’ strengths and weaknesses. For example, I think both Trump and Harris have issues that could make them vulnerable. For Trump, his past legal troubles and the general perception of his character could be a major liability. For Harris, her perceived lack of charisma and the baggage that comes with being the current Vice President could pose challenges. But, I'm not going to delve into the specifics of those potential problems. It's still way too early to make any kind of meaningful prediction. But I really think there are a few things that could swing things one way or the other.First, I think a lot will depend on the economic situation. If the economy is doing well and people feel optimistic about their financial futures, it’s going to swing the election in the incumbent’s favor. If people are struggling or just feel like things are generally headed in the wrong direction, then they're more likely to vote for change. And, as an engineer, I know that it’s always a long shot to predict exactly how the economy will go. But as far as I'm able to tell from what I've read, that could easily be the single most important factor. Another major factor will be voter turnout. Do either candidates have a significant base that they can bring to the polls? That can be a signiﬁcant factor in almost any election, and this one will probably be no different. And of course, it’s worth mentioning any unforeseen events. A major international crisis, a new scientific discovery, or any other major event can drastically reshuffle the deck and change the direction of any election. Also, both campaigns should be aware of the fact that political opinions are becoming more and more polarized. You're pretty unlikely to see a huge number of undecided voters who break one way or the other. So, to sum up, could Harris beat Trump? Sure, it's certainly possible. But just as easily, Trump could beat Harris. It's just going to depend on a lot of factors, many of which are impossible to anticipate. And with any luck, we will have an answer sooner rather than later.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? My immediate response is that it’s almost certainly a near-zero probability. Think about it: Our moon is a relatively large object compared to most moons in our solar system. And the Sun is a gigantic object - a thousand times the volume of Jupiter, and 333,000 times the mass of Earth! Now, the Sun is very, very far away, which is why it only appears to be the same size as the Moon in our sky. But if you crunch the numbers, you'll find that the odds of a moon appearing the same size as a star, given the size of the star and the planet, the planet's size, the moon's size, and the required orbital distance for all of that to line up is ridiculously small. You’d have to be talking about some sort of highly improbable accident. And even if you did get that alignment, it's not necessarily going to last very long. The orbits of celestial bodies aren’t perfectly stable. They're influenced by gravitational forces and even the pressure from solar winds. And the distances between them can drift over millions or billions of years. So even if such an arrangement were possible, it wouldn't be permanent.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? Okay, let's break this physics problem down. We're given two pieces of information: the weight of a body submerged in water (12N) and the weight of the water displaced by that same body (8N). These are the key ingredients we need to solve for the weight of the object in air.The fundamental principle at play here is Archimedes' principle. In short, an object submerged in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object. In this case, the buoyant force acting on the object in water is 8N, precisely the weight of the water displaced.Now, what happens when we put the object in air? Well, there's still buoyancy to consider, but it's vastly smaller due to the much lower density of air. We can essentially ignore it. So, the weight of an object in air is simply the object's actual weight, which is the sum of the buoyant force in water (8N) and the weight of the object in water (12N). Therefore, 8N + 12N = 20N.Putting it all together, the weight of that object in air is 20N. This is a classic example of using Archimedes' principle to determine an object’s true weight, given its weight in a fluid and the weight of the fluid it displaces. Pretty straightforward, right?

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. Well, there are a lot of factors at play, and it's a complex issue with no easy answers. For starters, the economic playing field has changed drastically. Women are far more likely to have careers, invest in education, and generally achieve economic self-sufficiency compared to previous generations. That provides a certain degree of independence that wasn't available before. Women have the agency to choose when they want to settle down, or whether they want to settle down at all. The pill, as an example, has also given women greater control over their bodies and reproductive choices, leading to a separation of sex and reproduction for the first time in history. Moreover, cultural norms have evolved too. There is less stigma associated with casual sex, cohabitation, and singlehood in recent years, and a new value is placed on individual satisfaction and personal growth. And finally, societal expectations, like a "ticking clock" to have children, are less intense, giving women the freedom to pursue their preferences. Given the vast array of possibilities made available to them, why wouldn't they want to see the world first?

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? Whether they're **redefining** or **redesigning** life is a matter of debate, but there's no question that scientists are actively engaged in genetic manipulation. And, yes, this is sometimes done with the explicit goal of making life "better," which leads us to the realm of genetic engineering, and more specifically, genetic modification, which is often used as a means to achieve that. For the purposes of this discussion, there is no material difference between these two activities. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) are pretty much everywhere these days. Think of modified crops with increased yields, plants that are resistant to pests, or plants that produce their own herbicides. It’s a long way from the days where a plant breeder would pollinate one plant with another using a brush, to where an organism’s specific genes can be altered with incredible precision. The tools available to scientists, such as CRISPR, allow for fine-tuned modifications that were previously unimaginable. As for *how*, the methods are continuously refined and advanced, but generally, it involves identifying a gene of interest, isolating it, and then integrating it into the target organism's genome. This can be done in a variety of ways, from using viruses as vectors to directly injecting the DNA into cells. Regardless of specifics, the underlying goal is to alter the information encoded in the DNA in a way that changes the organism's characteristics in some particular way. At each step, the focus is on improving the function of the new organism.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? It's a bit more complex than just a simple number of hours, I'm afraid. The amount of exercise you need to lose weight depends on a lot of factors, and there isn't a one-size-fits-all answer. One of the determining factors is your starting point. The more weight you have to lose, the more exercise you will need to do. Another key factor is your diet. You can't outrun a bad diet, as they say. Simply put, if you're consuming more calories than you're burning, you're not going to lose weight, regardless of how much time you spend exercising. People's metabolisms also differ from person to person. Some people burn calories more efficiently than others. Also, what type of exercises you do is a factor. A gentle stroll around the block for an hour won't burn nearly as many calories as an hour of high-intensity interval training (HIIT). And then of course, the intensity of those exercises is a factor. Someone who is extremely fit will be burning considerably more calories than someone just starting out. Your current fitness level plays a role as well. The body adapts to exercise over time, meaning that as you become fitter, your body becomes more efficient, burning fewer calories for the same activity. And let's not forget about consistency. Regular exercise is more important than sporadic, grueling workouts. Even a small amount of exercise, done consistently, is more beneficial than several hours of exercise per week that you skip the next week. So, to summarize, there are too many variables involved to give a definitive answer to the amount of exercise needed to lose weight. However, it is generally recommended that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity exercise per week, plus strength training twice a week. But again, this is just a general recommendation. It's best to consult with your doctor, and/or a certified trainer or dietician.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? No, and there never will be. It's a common misunderstanding of how evolution works, and that phrasing sets up a false dichotomy. The fish didn't just "decide" to walk onto land. Evolution doesn't work that way. It's not like there was some line of fish, and one day a fish raised its hand in a meeting and said, "I volunteer to be the first one to walk on land!" Instead, fish had adaptations already. Here’s an example: ABOVE: Tiktaalik roseae SOURCE: Wikipedia – Tiktaalik This is a fascinating fossil, found in the Canadian Arctic back in 2004. The fish lived roughly 375 million years ago. Unlike most fish, it had sturdy bones in its fins which could be used for support. It may have used those fins to prop itself up in shallow water or even pull itself along the shore. It also had a neck and a rib cage. So it’s not like there was a “fish” and a “man”. The process was much more gradual.

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? No. It's not even a matter of opinion. It's one of the fundamental axioms of arithmetic and mathematics in general: 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 1. While I am not a mathematician, I recall this axiom from my engineering studies.The problem is that in some of his rants on the subject, it sounds like he's not just trying to find the correct mathematical answer (1 x 1 = 1), but that he's attempting to redefine the whole system of arithmetic. He once described mathematics as "white male science" and that it "needs to be rethought". Honestly, I can’t find most of his rants even somewhat coherent, so I find it difficult to understand exactly what he’s trying to claim. But if I were forced to guess, I'd say that he thinks that because we're using the base-10 number system, that there's something inherently biased about that system.It's important to remember that math is a tool. You can't just redefine the whole system to suit your whims. It's like saying that you don't like a hammer, and therefore declaring that hammering doesn't work anymore. You can't just throw out all of the accumulated knowledge of centuries of scientific and mathematical advancements. The great thing about math, science, and engineering is that they're all built on top of one another. In math, these building blocks that we already know and agree on are called axioms, and by using axioms, we are able to solve incredibly complex problems. The mathematics and engineering of today are only possible because of the work of hundreds of thousands of people over centuries and the utilization of axioms.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? That's a fair question. The whole concept of gun control is, to some extent, trying to herd cats. People who are determined to get a gun, for whatever reason, are going to find a way. We can't pretend otherwise. ABOVE: Strikeforce Technologies, LLC - Hidden Guns, Hidden Pocket Guns, and Other Concealed Weapons This means that most gun control laws work by targeting the law-abiding citizens, not the criminals. The premise behind such laws is that restricting access to firearms will reduce gun violence overall. And there is some evidence to support this claim. Countries like Australia, with extremely strict gun control, have seen a dramatic drop in gun-related deaths. But a lot of that could be survivorship bias. Australia is a big, wealthy country, with a relatively small population and a culture that, for better or worse, isn't as 'gun-centric' as the United States. If gun control were the main factor in reducing gun violence, you'd expect to see similar results in other countries with tight restrictions, but that's not always the case. For example, a quick glance at Canada's gun violence statistics shows a mixed bag of results: ABOVE: Gun Violence Archive - Canada, 2023 The interesting thing about Canada is that their gun control laws are actually pretty strict, but it's still not as strict as Australia, and there are a lot more firearms in the civilian population. So it’s hard to say what to make of it. There are various ways to interpret what's going on in Canada. It's also worth noting that the United States is a huge country, with gun control laws varying widely from state to state. So the effect of different gun control measures is difficult to assess. States with stricter gun control do tend to see lower rates of gun violence, but there are just too many complicating factors to make a definitive conclusion. For instance, if the only way for criminals to obtain guns was the underground market, then that would suggest that stricter gun control measures would reduce illegal gun use. But there is evidence that people with criminal intent can obtain guns from a variety of sources, including straw purchases, theft, and the failure of background checks. And in the meantime, those laws may only disarm law-abiding citizens who aren't criminals in the first place.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? That’s an interesting question, but it's a bit of a trick to answer. The exact moment when a lineage switches from four legs to two isn't going to be clear-cut. What defines ‘walking’? At what point does an animal become bipedal; two-legged? Humans didn’t just suddenly pop out of the blue and start walking on two legs right away. ABOVE: Evolution of Bipedalism SOURCE: Anthropology.net But that’s the main point of the diagram: It wasn’t as clear cut as the diagram suggests. The ancestors of humans didn’t spend all their time on two legs. They spent some of their time on two legs and some of their time on all fours. These transitions can take millions of years. It's a gradual process that happened over many generations and many millions (or even hundreds of millions) of years. Maybe what you’re really looking for is, "Who was the final common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees?". But the answer to that is a mystery, and there is no good, reliable fossil evidence. The fact is, these types of fossils are extremely rare. And the farther back you go, the more difficult it is to find anything at all. The fossil record is incomplete, and we may never know the full details of what happened. Here's the problem. The fossil record is just a small window into the past.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? Well, as is sometimes the case, it depends on how you define the terms. It's certainly true that there are always going to be a lot of people who aren't particularly interested in complex thought, who prioritize immediate gratification, and who are relatively easily swayed by appeals to emotion. ABOVE: Bread and Circuses SOURCE: Pinterest But that doesn't mean that anti-intellectualism is *inevitable*. And it certainly *doesn't* mean that it's a good thing. The question is, in the current environment, what are the prevailing forces? Are there particular trends that are nudging this trend in one direction or another? My own observation is that there are a few factors in place today that are worth considering. One is the fragmentation of the media landscape. In the past, there were a relative handful of newspapers, three major television networks, and a few national magazines. So even if any particular outlet was biased, you still had lots of other outlets to compare against, as well as well-established editors and fact-checkers whose primary job was to ensure accuracy.

You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? Well, first off, the statement "Darwin Proved" is a bit of a misnomer. Darwin didn't "prove" anything, per se. What he did was propose a theory, a very well-supported theory, but still a theory, about the mechanism of natural selection. And from that theory, it follows that we are, in fact, animals. We share common ancestry with all other life on Earth, and we are subject to the same rules of evolution. So, I suppose he *implied* that we are all animals, but even the details of evolution were understood before him, by people like Buffon and his ideas about the transmutation of species. ABOVE SOURCE: Buffon’s Law, Principles, And Contributions. So yes, he implied it, and yes, the evidence overwhelmingly supports it. But as a scientist, Darwin was very skeptical of claims involving 'proof'. As a side note, Darwin was also very skeptical of claims involving 'the supernatural' and didn't make much mention of religion or spirituality in his work.Okay, so we *are* animals. And yes, it is true that most animals do not practice birth control, at least under current conditions. In natural settings, animals tend to breed until resource constraints limit them, such as food availability, habitat space, or the threat of predation. But we don't live in completely natural conditions. We have access to knowledge and technology that allow us to control our own reproduction. And also, we're dealing with "natural" in the sense of living in forests and following the sun, not "natural" compared to the way we live in a modern society.Humanity has evolved to be an incredibly adaptable species, capable of modifying its behavior and surroundings to maximize its chance of survival and reproduction. Birth control is simply another example of this adaptability, allowing us to balance reproduction with factors like family size, economic opportunity, and the overall quality of life. In a way, it's a very "human" thing to do.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? It depends. As an engineer, I tend to look at this from the perspective of physics. You are basically asking about taking two separate trips instead of one. In general, I'd say that it is better to take the single ultra-long haul flight. First off, there’s the obvious: you spend fewer hours in transit and are at your ultimate destination more quickly. Every time the engines on an aircraft are started, there's a lot of wear and tear. Think of it like your car; every trip has a high degree of wear and tear, with the number of miles driven having a less-than-proportional effect on damage. And in the case of the ultra-long haul flight, you only get that wear and tear once. On the other hand, consider the simple question of going to the restroom. On a 10-hour flight, you might have an opportunity to go every hour or so. On an 18-hour flight, such trips might need to be curtailed. So, from a comfort standpoint, one may be better than the other, depending on individual needs. Going along those lines, there's also jet lag to consider. The longer the trip, the more likely there is to be a significant time zone change, and therefore the bigger the jet lag is going to be. But in that case, it doesn’t matter whether there are two 10-hour flights or one 18-hour flight. Both will be roughly equivalent. And there's the issue of missed connections. If one of those 10-hour flights is delayed, it might cause one to miss their second flight, leading to even more wasted time and stress. But overall, the ultra-long haul flight seems to be better. However, there is one more point: the chances of serious injury or death from a plane crash are so low that the impact of one additional flight is virtually nothing.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? As a matter of fact, yes. Despite my general disdain for purposefully bad grammar, there are indeed occasions where it's not only acceptable but even preferable to deviate from what's considered "perfect" English. It's a multifaceted issue, really, and the answer depends heavily on context and purpose. One instance is when you're deliberately trying to evoke a specific mood or persona. For instance, if you're a writer crafting a character who is meant to be uneducated or even a bit slow-witted, using simplified grammar and slang can be an effective way to bring that character to life. It's about creating verisimilitude, that feeling of authenticity. Similarly, if you're trying to mimic a particular regional dialect, you're going to have to adjust from the standard, which can involve grammar shifts and unique vocabularies.Another instance is when you’re specifically aiming to connect with a distinct audience. Imagine, for example, communicating with someone who has a different first language, particularly if your ability to speak their language perfectly is limited. In that case, it’s usually better to use simple structures and common words to ensure the listener understands the overall message. Or, in the ever-evolving landscape of internet lingo, the use of intentional misspellings or shorthand can sometimes be helpful. Lastly, there are times when a level of informality might be useful to convey a more genuine, personal connection with another person.

What movies were marketed in a very misleading way, making the audience expect something different from what was presented? The most egregious example that comes to mind is *Sucker Punch*. It was marketed as a non-stop action movie – the kind of film that would be right at home amongst the other macho blockbusters of the time. The trailers were a series of increasingly loud and flashy video clips: explosions, gunfire, and scantily-clad women. And the film does indeed feature an appreciable amount of action. But the trailers hid the vast majority of the story. The film's protagonist, Baby Doll, is committed to a mental institution and effectively uses her imagination and fantasies to escape the horrors of her real-world circumstances. And the scenes of action are all part of this imaginative world. The result is a movie that is much more cerebral and introspective than the trailer would have you believe. To me, it felt like a brilliant bait-and-switch, and I enjoyed the movie a good deal. But I can fully appreciate how others would have been very frustrated by the experience. Then there's the case of *Drive*. The trailer for this film featured a fast car, cool music, and a brooding Ryan Gosling. It gave off a general sense of it being similar to a car-chase movie, akin to the *Fast And Furious* franchise. And I can understand how audiences would be confused. The film is much more about mood and atmosphere and is not the action-packed film that was marketed to the public. I can also see how people would have been misled. Even though I, personally, liked the movie, I can imagine it would be a letdown for someone expecting to see Vin Diesel.

What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Darwin’s *On the Origin of Species* lays out an incredibly detailed case for natural selection, so it's kind of hard to summarize it. However, that doesn’t mean I can’t try. The fundamental premise is pretty straightforward: populations of organisms change over time. And the mechanism driving this change is what Darwin termed "natural selection." The basic idea is that, within any population, there is a variety of traits. Some of these traits are heritable, i.e., passed down from parent to offspring. And within that population, different individuals have different levels of reproductive success due to the specific traits they possess. This leads to a gradual change in the frequency of those heritable traits over time. For example, if a giraffe is born with a slightly longer neck, and that provides an advantage in reaching high-up leaves, that giraffe and its offspring are more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on that long-neck trait. But Darwin wasn't just arguing that things change over time. He also argued that all of life had a common ancestry, that all living creatures were connected via common descent. To back this up, Darwin presented a wealth of evidence from different fields. First, he drew on the fossil record, showing how fossil organisms changed over time, and even tracing out probable lineage. The fossil record, though incomplete, displayed a chronological progression of life forms. For example, some ancient fossils show clear similarities with living species, implying a history of change. In modern times, advancements in radiometric dating techniques and more complete fossil records of some of the most exciting finds have helped solidify Darwin's findings. Another piece of evidence comes from comparative anatomy. Darwin pointed out that seemingly different organisms often share similar structural elements. This is especially true for the limbs of different animals, showing a pattern of common ancestry. The similarity in the underlying bone structure of the human arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper, and a bird’s wing speaks volumes. Furthermore, Darwin utilized embryology, studying the developmental stages of various organisms. He showed that these early stages often reveal common traits that are less apparent in the adult forms. For example, the embryos of many vertebrates, including humans, share characteristics like gill slits and tails. Another key piece of evidence came from the study of biogeography, that is, the geographic distribution of species. His observations of the flora and fauna on the Galapagos Islands were a cornerstone of his argument. The unique species on those islands, closely related but distinct from those on the mainland, provided compelling evidence for adaptation and diversification in isolation. Darwin also looked at the experiments and observations of animal and plant breeders. He noted that through artificial selection, humans could influence the traits of organisms by choosing which individuals reproduce. These practical observations showed that traits are heritable, and by manipulating the traits, it was possible to select for changes that led to distinct new varieties.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? Yes, airplanes sometimes *do* have to forgo storing fuel in their tanks because of weight restrictions. It isn’t a particularly common occurrence in the commercial airline industry, where the goal is typically to carry as much fuel as possible. This is for a variety of reasons: in general, it's cheaper fuel from a particular hub and/or to simply avoid having to refuel as frequently. But for some aircraft, weight savings is absolutely paramount, and fuel storage capacity may be dialed back accordingly.Let's consider the alternatives, then. The most obvious is fuel bladders. These are, effectively, massive, flexible bags that conform to whatever space they're stored in, and are frequently used in military aircraft and some general aviation applications to maximize fuel capacity. However, they have the obvious downside of taking up valuable cargo or passenger space, and they do have some inherent vulnerabilities (though improvements in material science have made them quite durable). Fuel bladders are often chosen for military and civilian rescue operations because of the ability to quickly adapt an aircraft for a longer flight.The other obvious solution, albeit one that's not nearly as common, is to utilize external fuel tanks. It's pretty straightforward: put a fuel tank on the outside of the aircraft, usually under the wings or along the fuselage. This has the benefit of not taking up any of the precious internal space. But, of course, it also dramatically increases drag and thereby reduces the aircraft's efficiency, so it’s a trade-off. You wouldn't use it for commercial aviation, but external tanks are common in military aircraft for extending range. Weight considerations during the design process for a new aircraft model are a delicate balance, and there is no blanket rule for deciding between internal tanks, fuel bladders, or external tanks, or any combination thereof. It's a complex equation with many variables.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? That's a good question, and one that's been the subject of much debate and speculation. The short answer is that it's highly, highly unlikely. Let's consider just a few of the logistical problems involved. A common estimate is that the Ark would have needed to accommodate two of every animal species on Earth, or seven pairs of the "clean" animals (as well as provisions for both the animals and the humans). Even if we assume some level of "kinds" instead of "species," which would probably still lead to a great many animals needing shelter, there simply wouldn't have been enough room. The dimensions of the Ark are given in the Bible (Genesis 6:15) as 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high, which translates to something like 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. Assuming we can trust those measurements, that’s still a sizable vessel, about the size of a container ship, which is pretty big, but the Ark also had to house the animals, and all the food, and all the water—for over a year; that's a lot of supplies. ABOVE: The size of the ark relative to a modern ship SOURCE: Wikipedia - Noah's Ark There are quite a few credible scientific studies that have been done that consider this problem.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? It's an interesting hypothetical scenario, and the answer depends on a lot of factors, mostly related to how much electricity bikes could realistically generate, and how much electricity people use in the first place. First of all: how much electricity do bicycles actually generate? I'll admit, I don't actually know this off the top of my head. A quick search for “wattage of electric bicycle” turns up a lot of conflicting information, depending on the type of electric bicycle, the grade, and so on. And also the rider’s level of effort. But for a normal electric bicycle, it looks like the range is somewhere around 250 to 750 watts. A quick search for "human power generation watts" produces results like this: ABOVE: Human Power Generation (Watts) SOURCE: Watts and Human Output So maybe an average of 100 watts for each hour of cycling is a reasonable estimate. How much electricity does humanity use in a year? That's another tricky question. If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? That's a good question. The term 'burger' has definitely expanded over the years. I mean, if we're being strict, a burger is a patty of ground meat, usually beef, served on a bun. That’s it. But the definition has blurred, hasn't it? These days, you've got veggie burgers, turkey burgers, even breakfast burgers. Even beyond “burger” itself we are seeing a blurring of categorical definitions -- just consider "chicken tenders". Do those count if they are breaded chunks of chicken thigh, or are they chicken fingers if they are breaded chicken breast? It seems that as long as you have a sandwich on a bun, the content of the burger patty doesn’t matter all that much, and can include many ingredients. So, it seems fair to say that the "burger" category now includes sandwiches with fish or chicken patties.But as soon as you go beyond patties on buns, and consider all the different sandwich fillings that are possible... that's where the real question comes in. At what point does a sandwich stop being a burger, and start being something else entirely? Suppose, for arguments sake, that one were to put a slice of smoked salmon on a croissant with cream cheese and dill, and then just call THAT a burger. Or maybe a crab cake on sourdough. Or what if, instead of the bun, the sandwich is using two slices of pizza to hold the filling? The possibilities become endless. So, I guess my answer is... it all boils down to convention. There is no hard boundary between a burger and other sandwiches. Like so many things in language, the meaning of the word "burger" is constantly evolving.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? Well, yeah. Quite a few, actually. First of all, even if we assume that such a submarine were possible (which is a pretty big assumption), the materials necessary to withstand that kind of pressure, let alone the water itself, would be a colossal engineering challenge. The forces exerted at that depth are simply immense. Then comes the issue of the generator. Eighty thousand PSI is a staggering amount of force. I'm not even sure if currently existing technology could achieve such a thing, and if it could, its tolerances would be incredibly tight. And then you’ve got the energy conversion itself. The conversion efficiency would need to be extremely high to make this worthwhile. You're starting with one gallon of water, using it somehow to generate an enormous amount of energy, and then using some of that energy to extract hydrogen. And that extracted hydrogen would need to be piped to the surface somehow. One gallon of water, even if you could extract all the hydrogen, does not amount to a whole lot of energy on the surface. It's just not a sustainable energy model. So, at every step of the way, from the pressures involved to the energy equations, there are significant practical and physical limitations to this thought experiment.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? Alright, I’ll give that a shot. From the outset, let me preface this by saying that this is coming from an atheist's perspective, from my own personal interpretation of the world. I find the question interesting because it's often thrown at atheists as some sort of gotcha, as if the lack of a belief in a god somehow negates the existence or importance of moral principles. And it’s true, if you're religious, you have a straightforward explanation: a deity instilled morality in humans or gave them a way to discover it through revelation or other means. But, as an atheist, I have to explain morality using natural, observable processes. So, where does morality come from for me? I see it as a product of evolution, culture, and personal experience. Humans, being social animals, benefited from the development of social behaviors that allowed for cooperation and survival. Those who cooperated and formed societies were more likely to pass on their genes.And I suspect this same evolutionary process is responsible for empathy, the ability to feel the pain of others, which is a powerful motivator for moral behavior. Now, I don't want to reduce all morality down to pure biology. Culture is also vital. Societal rules, norms, and laws evolve over time, providing a framework for behavior. These cultural norms can influence individual behavior and conscience, and in turn, those behaviors and values adapt and alter the culture in a feedback loop. Finally, there's personal experience. Growing up, I learned from my family, my friends, and my teachers, and from my own mistakes. I developed a sense of right and wrong, learned from the ways I was treated as a child and the consequences of my own actions after I grew up. These experiences shape our individual moral compasses. So for me, the concept of conscience isn't some divinely bestowed gift, but a complex phenomenon that emerges from a combination of evolved traits, societal expectations, and individual experiences. It's always evolving.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? This question brings up all sorts of difficult issues, and there's really no easy answer. On the one hand, you have freedom of religion, which is a fundamental right in many countries, including the United States. Religious organizations have the right to practice their faith, and, from their point of view, that would include the right to only hire people who share their beliefs. It's hard to expect a church, for example, to hire a person who is openly antagonistic toward their faith, and then expect that organization to function properly. You would think it would be very difficult for an Atheist to perform the function of a pastor. Even if the person were just neutral -- not even questioning the religious beliefs -- that certainly seems like it would be an awkward situation. On the other hand, requiring an organization to hire employees who don't share their beliefs can be seen as a form of discrimination, and many people believe that everyone, regardless of their religious beliefs, deserves equal opportunity in the workplace. This is a particularly potent issue to many people, and some would argue that it’s simply wrong for a religious organization to receive preferential treatment in hiring practices. In the United States, there are legal precedents about these types of issues, but they are inconsistent. For example, the Supreme Court has ruled that religious organizations are exempt from certain anti-discrimination laws when it comes to their ministers or pastors. So, they can discriminate based on religion in those cases. But there are other types of employees, such as teachers at a religious school or administrative staff, where the courts have taken a different view. It gets really messy when we start talking about what constitutes "religious" activities, and to what extent.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? It's a good question. You’ll see a lot of different takes tossed around on the subject. Everyone has their own pet theories. Some people blame the moderators, others the users. Some say it's because the high-quality content creators have moved on. Others claim the platform was always a dumpster fire, we just didn't realize it. There's probably truth in all those claims and more. The most common talking point you'll find is that the quality of answers has declined. In the beginning, you’d see answers from actual experts. Now, you're more likely to wade through mountains of simplistic, often wrong or misleading, answers. Take the topic of evolution, for instance. You'll occasionally find some pretty solid answers. But you are more likely find absolute garbage from know-nothings who just watched a few YouTube videos and think they're suddenly an expert on the subject. In my experience, the people who write the most confidently and are the least knowledgeable. And there's always a crowd of folks eager to pile on, especially if you make a point that challenges their current world view.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? I'm not sure what more I can say to convince people to provide evidence. It's just a basic requirement for rational belief, and yet it seems to be routinely ignored. I'm always open-minded, and if someone can provide a piece of evidence to convince me, I'll gladly change my beliefs. But until then, I'm sticking with what I already know. Of course, there are things I don't know, and I am open to the possibility that I am wrong. I just need to see the evidence first, the same as when I'm evaluating claims in engineering. If someone wants to propose a theory or build a machine, they better be well-grounded in the principles of physics and provide evidence that supports their design. It's just common sense. The same thing goes with worldviews. If you want me to believe in a non-theistic worldview, you need to provide the evidence. Otherwise, I'm not likely to believe it.

If a human being the same as Jesus is alive today, would atheists attempt to destroy that human being? That's a tricky hypothetical, laden with presuppositions. But let's break it down, step by step. First off, we're assuming a human being, genetically identical to Jesus, exists. That automatically triggers a host of religious and philosophical questions. Would this individual possess any divine abilities? Would they remember their past life? Or would they be just another human, destined to be judged on their actions in the here and now? Next, we have to consider the premise of atheists attempting to destroy this person. Surely it's a generalization to paint all atheists with the same brush. The motivations of atheists are as diverse as the motivations of theists. Some atheists might express a strong conviction about their disbelief, arguing that this person is a fraud. Others might express indifference. Still others might be intrigued, eager to dissect and analyze this individual’s existence through the lens of science and reason. And then, of course, there's the question of whether the human being, our Jesus clone, might pose enough of a threat to garner ire from some atheists that would lead to violence? If the person starts making religious claims, there might be a few atheists who would seek to discredit them, just as there is plenty of criticism of religious leaders. There is a range of actions that people take when someone annoys them; but destroying a human being would be a clear violation of the law for anyone, atheist or otherwise. But that's not the question, is it? The question is whether atheists would *attempt* to destroy this person, not whether they would succeed. Given the legal and social constraints, I think the answer is probably no.

At what age does interest in video games usually decline? I don’t know that there's any specific age where interest in video games *usually* declines, but it's a question I hear quite a bit from my daughter and her friends these days. I'm sure it varies from person to person, but I have a few thoughts on the matter. First, as people get older, they encounter more and more responsibilities, like work, family, and other commitments. They tend to have less time for leisure activities, and that includes video games. Second, people's interests tend to evolve as they get older. What someone finds enjoyable in their teens might not be as appealing in their 30s or 40s. People might start to prefer different forms of entertainment, such as movies, sports, or traveling, over video games.I also suspect that the availability of different games might play a role. Back when I was growing up, video games were a brand new medium, and the choices were somewhat limited. Now, there are an endless number of games available across a huge range of genres, and it's hard to keep up. There's always something new coming out. And while younger people are generally more adept at picking up new games, older people might find the constant changes and new mechanics overwhelming. In my case, I can play a few games with my daughter and enjoy them, but I don't have the time or inclination to stay up with the latest trends. Though I suspect there are plenty of people out there my age and older who still thoroughly enjoy video games as much as they ever did.

Are most atheists evil? No, most atheists are not evil. That’s a pretty ridiculous claim, and it’s completely at odds with my own experience and everything else I've read on the subject. I'm not an atheist, so I can’t claim to be an authority on their worldview or motivations. But I have known plenty of atheists over the course of my life, and they’re just as varied as the rest of the population. Some are good people, some are bad people, and most fall somewhere in between. There's no discernible pattern that I've been able to detect.I do find it interesting that people often assume that if someone doesn’t believe in a god, then they must automatically be immoral. As if belief in a higher power is the only thing that can possibly stop a person from going on a crime spree. Even if it were true that atheists are more likely to commit crimes (which, to be clear, it is not), it would still be impossible to know if their lack of belief in a god was the cause. It could be any number of confounding factors, such as poverty, lack of education, mental health problems, or a whole host of other considerations.But again, I just don’t buy it. I’ve seen plenty of religious people do terrible things in the name of their faith, so I don’t think there’s any particular philosophical system that guarantees that someone will be a good person. In the end, it all comes down to the individual. People are people, and no two are exactly alike.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? That's a bit of a trick question if I've ever heard one. The answer depends on how you want to define a 'sandwich'. Obviously, bread is the foundation. Then you have the fillings, and anything goes there. So the 'main' ingredient is really the protein used in the filling, whether that's turkey, roast beef, or even something like a portobello mushroom. ABOVE: Sandwich diagram SOURCE: I made it Now if you were to ask me for a more interesting question, I'd want to know what constitutes a 'sandwich' in the first place. Is a hot dog a sandwich? What about a taco? There are some pretty heated debates on the topic. But for my own definition, the meat needs to be wedged between two pieces of bread. That's it. So while the bread might be the most important part, the meat is the main ingredient. But in the end, it all comes down to personal preference.

Do atheists know God is WATCHING them? I’m not sure what you mean by “watching”. Are you asking if atheists believe in some sort of cosmic accounting system, where a god is always monitoring their behavior and keeping track of who’s naughty and who’s nice? If so, then the answer is a definitive no. A core tenet of atheism is a lack of belief in a god or gods, including one that’s constantly peering down from the heavens, scrutinizing our every action. But if you’re asking a different question, such as whether atheists consider the consequences of their actions, then the answer is an obvious yes. Atheists, like anyone else, understand that their choices have repercussions. They recognize that their actions can bring about rewards or punishments, not through some divine judgment but through the natural interplay of cause and effect. They understand that treating others with kindness and respect often leads to positive outcomes, both for themselves and for those around them. They also know that breaking laws or engaging in harmful behaviors can lead to negative consequences, such as imprisonment or social isolation. So in this sense, atheists are very aware of their actions, and they carefully consider the potential outcomes.

When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter? No, not exactly. It's a bit of a linguistic simplification, but ultimately, the answer is no. The law of conservation of mass, or more broadly, the law of conservation of energy, holds true. What's happening is a complete conversion of mass into other forms of energy, but not actual annihilation. The equation most famously associated with this process is E=mc², where 'E' represents energy, 'm' is mass, and 'c' is the speed of light. As you can see, a bit of mass 'm', can be converted into a huge amount of energy 'E', because 'c' is a very large number. And in fact, that's all that's happening. The mass isn't being destroyed, just converted. The energy is still there, whether it is in the form of kinetic energy, heat, or newly formed particles. So, it's not that the matter is destroyed, it's just being changed into something else, which is still subject to the law of conservation of energy. The particles themselves, such as an electron and its antiparticle counterpart, the positron, are still there, just in the form of energy. You can think of it much like the way you can convert one form of energy into another--electrical energy into heat energy, for example. It’s still energy, just in a different form. And finally, you have to keep in mind the difference between mass and matter as the terms are used in physics. Matter is often used to describe the particles themselves, while mass is a measure of their resistance to acceleration.

How can I share the life eternal with those that refuse to view it today? It is like giving someone a check for a billion dollars and they refuse to cash it. There's no easy answer, of course. But if someone isn't interested, what can you do? You can't force them to take up your offer. I’m reminded of the old saying, "You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make him drink." And I would also add that I'm not really interested in being pushy anyway. I have had various people try to convince me of things over the years. And the only thing more certain than death and taxes is that most of them, if they were to come across me again, would try to say things like "See? I told you so!" I don’t want to put anyone in that position. So if someone isn't interested, I just let it go. Then, by example, demonstrate that this life is worth having. If someone is genuinely interested, it won't be hard for them to see. The problem is that most people don't even know what they're looking for. They have superficial goals that satisfy for a short while, but ultimately leave them empty. People want fame, they want money, they want the approval of others. But those things don't last. Sure, they make you feel good for a little bit, and that's important, but eventually those feelings fade. And then what? You're back to square one. I, personally, have found something that offers a much more profound and lasting satisfaction. It's not something that can be easily explained, because it's not something easily understood. It's a lot like being in love if you've ever been there. The best anyone can do is to describe what it *feels* like. And even then, it’s not really the same. The listener will need a lot of imagination.

Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? Yes, the idea stems from a literal interpretation of the Bible. Specifically, it's derived from calculating the lifespans of the patriarchs listed in the Book of Genesis, the foundation of the Jewish and Christian faiths. These accounts are typically used to construct a timeline that places the creation of the world at roughly 6,000 years ago.It's important to mention that this timeline requires a specific understanding of the Bible. Not all religious people agree with this literal interpretation for a variety of reasons. Some interpret the Genesis creation stories as allegorical or symbolic, while others believe in long periods of time. And of course, anyone who accepts the science of geology and evolution knows that the earth is much older than 6,000 years. But strictly speaking, yes, the 6,000 year estimate comes from a literal reading of Genesis. Above: A page from a bible. SOURCE: Pinterest.com

Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory? First, before I answer, I'm going to cop out a bit and say that it's impossible to say *why* people believe the things they do. But, I've got a few ideas about what might be going on. The first is that it's pretty much the standard strategy to blame the other side for anything bad that happens. Let's say that COVID-19 did come from the Wuhan lab. Well, the obvious next step would be to find out *why* and *how* it happened. And if that happened, the next step would be to try to pin the blame on somebody. And, obviously, the political right is going to try to pin the blame on the left. Of course. That's just how things work. The second idea is that if the virus *did* come from the lab, then that would be a bit embarrassing for the people who were working in that lab, and the people who were funding them. And I suspect that there are a lot of people who don't want to revisit those particular details, including the exact mechanisms that allowed the virus to escape its containment, who was involved, etc. And it's just a lot easier on everyone to simply deny that it happened.

Could you beat up your 20 year old self? I suspect not, or at least, it would be a difficult (and inadvisable) task. I've seen some of the guys down at the gym, and I wouldn't take them on right now. And I’m a lot older now than 20. On the other hand, when I was 20, when I was still actively playing ice hockey, I was in much better shape. I was more agile and coordinated too. As I've gotten older, I've mostly traded away those abilities for the ability to sit in a chair all day and do complex calculations and modeling on a computer. I'm no couch potato, and I do try to get on the treadmill a few times a week. But on the other hand, back then, I was on the ice at least two times a week. I was more flexible too, or at least had much better range of motion. I could certainly skate very fast in those days, and I had good endurance. It’s a bit of a moot point, as you can't really go back in time and fight yourself. But let's say that I did actually manage to find a time machine (I’m an engineer; it’s a common fantasy) and could actually go back and square off against myself when I was 20. I would probably lose, even now.

How has technology changed our lives? Technology has changed our lives in countless ways, far too many to comprehensively list here, but I'll try to hit the highlights. Firstly, consider communication. Before the advent of the internet and mobile phones, staying in touch with people who lived far away was a much more laborious and expensive process. You relied on letters, which took days if not weeks to arrive, or expensive long-distance phone calls. Today, we can instantly communicate with anyone around the globe via email, text, video calls, and social media. ABOVE: A somewhat dated image of a rotary phone. SOURCE: Wikipedia. Beyond the immediate benefits of increased and instantaneous communication, this has also led to a more globalized world, where it's easier for people from different cultures to interact and share ideas. This, in turn, has fostered a greater understanding and appreciation of different perspectives. But the pace of technological change has also accelerated, leading us to a present day where we are now experiencing a bit of a backlash. Consider the rise of misinformation and echo chambers. The same tools that allow us to connect so easily also contribute to the rapid spread of false or misleading information. Social media algorithms, designed to keep us engaged, can also create filter bubbles, reinforcing our existing biases and limiting our exposure to diverse viewpoints. This isn't to say that these technologies are inherently bad, but we're certainly seeing the downsides of them. I mean, I can’t even remember the land-line phone number of my own parents. So there are certainly some benefits to technological progress.

Do you eat seafood? What is your favorite fish to eat? Yes, I do eat seafood, although not as often as I probably should. My favorites are probably those ubiquitous ones, like salmon or tuna. But I’m also a sucker for a good plate of fried calamari, or maybe some grilled scallops. If I'm in the mood for something a bit more adventurous, I'll go for some blackened redfish or maybe even some sushi grade yellowtail. I suppose if I had to pick a single favorite, it might be the tuna, but I'd be hard pressed to be able to specifically quantify which one is better. It would also depend a lot on how it's prepared. A good seared tuna steak can be hard to beat. But then again, good sushi grade tuna is also tough to top. And of course, the best seafood is only going to be as good as its freshness. You can tell the difference between fresh and not-so-fresh seafood in an instant. You can also usually tell when it was frozen and thawed out repeatedly – the texture is going to be all wrong. Really, the best seafood is going to come from places that are right on the coast. So, if I’m visiting the coast and am presented with a good plate of fresh seafood, I’ll usually leap at the chance.
